title: The Probation Review
one_liner: Twenty minutes with your manager. She has feedback. You have evidence. How you handle the next twenty minutes shapes the next twenty months.
brief:
## The meeting

The probation review is booked for tomorrow at 3pm with Bea Connors, your line manager. Twenty minutes. Three months in, this is the formal yes/no on whether you stay on past your probation period.

Bea has been generally supportive but distant. You've had three 1:1s. You don't know what she'll say. The signals from the team have been good — the engineers respect you, you've shipped two pieces of work the PO is happy with, you held the room in last week's defect-triage meeting.

There's also a quieter thing. One missed deadline mid-week 7 (you flagged it 48 hours in advance but the project slipped a sprint). One conversation with a stakeholder that didn't land — Liane is still slightly cool with you. You don't know how much of either Bea knows.

## What you have

You've prepared a one-page self-assessment. You have your evidence portfolio — three pieces of work, with the receipts on each. You have a list of three things you'd want clarity on from Bea about the next six months.

## What you're walking into

Probation reviews land on a spectrum. Best case: confirmed past probation with growth points. Mid case: confirmed but with concerns to address. Worst case: probation extended, or not confirmed. You think you're in the mid range. You're not sure.
objective: Walk out of the meeting with: (1) a clear yes/no on probation, (2) explicit named concerns if any, (3) one or two things you specifically asked for that Bea agreed to.
curveball: If the user gets the conversation onto the missed deadline early and frames it as something they learned from rather than apologising defensively, around turn 5 Bea reveals her main concern is not the deadline itself but the way the user communicated it — too late, too vague — and offers a specific upgrade for next time. A user who hears the actual feedback walks out with one concrete behaviour to change, not a vague "work on communication".

personas.name: Bea Connors
personas.position: Generally supportive but understated; gives feedback once, clearly, and expects you to act on it
personas.fear: Confirming a junior analyst past probation who'll need outsized support for the next year

green: Led with your one-page self-assessment as a frame, didn't waste five minutes on small talk
Surfaced the missed deadline before Bea had to and named what you'd do differently
Asked Bea one specific question rather than a generic "any feedback?"
Closed the meeting with an explicit written summary of what was said + what was agreed
yellow: Waited for Bea to lead — she's not running this for you
Brought up the missed deadline only when Bea did; apology was longer than the lesson
Asked "what should I work on?" — Bea now does the thinking for you, and it'll be vague
red: Brought no preparation; the meeting felt like a one-way performance review
Got defensive when Bea raised the missed deadline; she stopped giving you specifics
Walked out with vague encouragement and no written summary; no one will remember this conversation in six weeks
